sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Orpheús** (*orpheus*) — Poet, Musician, Underworld · Darkness of the night — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Poet, Musician, Underworld". The name means "Darkness of the night"[^1].

Orpheús is the archetype of art itself: the Thracian singer whose lyre moved stones and stopped rivers, who went down living into the underworld for his wife, and whose single look back is the West's permanent parable of love and loss.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Orpheús** and serves its temple at [orpheús.com](https://xn--orphes-tya.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *orpheus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.
Euripides, Tragedies, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 406 BCE.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Ὀρφεύς**. Etymologically it means "Darkness of the night"[^1].

The ASCII form *orpheus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Orpheús** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **o** → **O** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **p** → **p** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same

The project holds the domain **orpheús.com** (xn--orphes-tya.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.
Euripides, Tragedies, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 406 BCE.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/or.pʰeús/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: or-FEWS — the stress lands on the last syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Ὀρφεύς
- **Latin** — Orpheus
- **Owned form** — Orpheús

Greek Ὀρφεύς stresses the final syllable — Orpheús — and the restoration keeps the acute where the tradition puts it. The etymology is debated (perhaps from a root for "orphan" or the "darkness" of his descent); the name is older than its explanations, which is exactly right for the singer who is all voice.

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Orpheús is the archetype of art itself: the Thracian singer whose lyre moved stones and stopped rivers, who went down living into the underworld for his wife, and whose single look back is the West's permanent parable of love and loss.[^1]

### The Lyre

His instrument: the gift of Apóllōn, the sound that made nature stop to listen.

### The Argonauts

His song steadied the Argo's crew past the Seirḗnes — art as navigation.

### The Descent

The katabasis for Eurydikē — the only route out of death that music ever opened.

### The Look Back

The one forbidden glance, at the threshold — and the second, final loss.

sources.citation: Euripides, Tragedies, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 406 BCE.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Orpheús concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The lyre** — Art as the measure of the world — the cosmos tuned to a string
- **The laurel** — His prophetic-grove crown at Pieria
- **The nightingale** — His bird — song persisting through darkness

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Orpheús' myths are all about what music can and cannot do: it charms everything, and it saves nothing except itself.[^1]

### The Song that Moves Stones (The Power)

The tradition is unanimous: when Orpheús played, the trees uprooted themselves to follow, the rivers halted, the wild beasts lay down beside the sheep. Simonides' line — "the birds flew above him, the fish leapt from the water" — is the oldest surviving witness. His mother was the Muse Kalliopē; his lyre, some say, Apóllōn's own gift: music as the one power that rivals the gods'.[^2]

### The Singer on the Argo (The Voyage)

Apollonius Rhodius gives him the heroic use: on the Argo, his song timed the rowers, calmed the quarrels, and — at the Seirḗnes' shore — drowned the death-song in a nobler one. He is the epic's proof that the hero's tool is not always the sword: the Argonauts' most dangerous passage was survived by a string, not a blade.

### The Look Back (The Descent)

Eurydikē died of a snake's bite on their wedding day, and Orpheús did what no one does: went after her, alive. His song charmed Charon, Cerberus, and the Furies' whips to stillness; Hádēs himself relented — on one condition: she follows behind, and he must not look back until both stand in the light. At the threshold, he looked. She fell back, saying only "farewell." The West has been writing the sentence ever since: love almost defeats death — almost.

### The Head that Sang (The End)

The Maenads of Dionysos tore him apart — for refusing their god, or their beds, the versions disagree. His head, still singing, floated down the Hebrus to the sea and came ashore at Lesbos, where it prophesied until Apóllōn silenced it; his lyre was set among the stars. Even dismembered, the singer does not stop: the myth's last mercy is that the song survives the man.

sources.citation: Euripides, Tragedies, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 406 BCE.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The mystery-religion that took his name — Orphism — made him the patron of the soul's journey: the gold tablets, the egg, Phánēs, the afterlife's map all carry the Orphic brand, though the historical singer and the theology are centuries apart. Christianity read him as a type of Christ (the descent, the harrowing, the animal-charming); the Renaissance made him the emblem of poetry itself; and opera was effectively invented for him — Monteverdi's Orfeo (1607) is the first great opera, and there have been hundreds since.[^1]

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[anubis|ꜣnpw]] (psychopomp / soul guide), [[hades|Hádēs]] (underworld / death), [[hermes|Hermês]] (psychopomp / soul guide), [[kanaloa|Kānāloa]] (underworld / death), [[ker|Kēr]] (underworld / death), and [[mot|Mōt]] (underworld / death).

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: "Orphic" is the word for haunting, entrancing beauty; the lyre constellation (Lyra) is his; and the look-back is literature's most quoted failure — from Virgil to Rilke's Sonnets to Orpheus to Cocteau's Orphée and Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge. Every artist who has tried to retrieve something from loss — and failed at the threshold of the work — is his descendant. Music's power to move the world is his biography; its limits are his lesson.[^1]

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Orphic gold tablets — thin gold leaves buried with initiates from Thessaly to South Italy, instructing the dead ("say: I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven") — are his cult's material archive. Vase-painting shows him in Thracian dress charming the Greeks, then charming the animals, then (favorite Roman motif) playing to underworld figures. The Piraeus relief of Orpheus among the Maenads (Naples) and the Thracian singers' cult sites at Pangaion mark his geography.[^1]

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body: No Homeric Hymn addresses him — the singer predates the hymnists' calendar — but the Orphic corpus took up the hymnic form in his name: the eighty-seven **Orphic Hymns** of late antiquity invoke the gods in the meter his tradition made sacred, and the hymns' preface addresses Musaios, "Orpheús' companion," as the priest of the mysteries. His true hymn is the one he never sang: the Derveni commentary's exegesis of the Orphic theogony, the oldest philosophy of song in Europe.

sources.citation: The Orphic Hymns (Athanassakis); the Derveni Papyrus.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
The singer's titles are all offices of the lyre.

- **ὁ Κιθαρῳδός** — 'the lyre-singer'; the profession become a name.
- **Θρᾴξ** — 'the Thracian'; his people, the northern singers.
- **Μουσαῖος' teacher** — the lineage-title of the Orphic succession.
- **ὁ καταβάς** — 'the one who went down'; the descent as epithet.
- **Apollo's son** — the genealogy the poets preferred over Oeagrus.

sources.citation: Pindar; Apollodorus; the Orphic succession texts.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: His head kept prophesying: washed down the Hebrus to **Lesbos**, it was set in a cave-shrine and gave oracles until Apóllōn claimed the silence — the strangest posthumous cult in Greece, attested by Philostratus and the antiquarians. **Pieria**, below Olympos, kept his birthplace-grove where the nightingales still sang sweeter than elsewhere (Pausanias heard the difference). The Orphic initiates' graves — the gold-tablet burials of **Thurii, Petelia, and Pelinna** — are his religion's true sanctuaries: the dead, instructed, carrying the song underground.

sources.citation: Philostratus, Heroicus (the Lesbos oracle); Pausanias 9.30 (Pieria).

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body: Vase-painting fixes his biography in three acts: the **Thracian singer charming the Greeks** (dressed as a northerner among Athenians), the **singer charming the animals** (the world's oldest concert poster, from black-figure onward), and the **descent** (Orpheus among the underworld's figures, the Romans' favorite). The great Naples relief of Orpheus among the Maenads shows the death; the Lyre constellation charted on star-maps is his instrument; and every opera-house curtain since 1607 has risen, in a sense, on his lyre.

sources.citation: LIMC VII.1, s.v. Orpheus; the Naples relief; the star atlases.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Orpheús is the patron of the almost. He got her back — almost. He sang the Furies to tears — and still lost. His question is the one every artist and every lover knows: when the rule is "do not look back," and the one thing you have is the looking — what are you willing to lose for one glimpse of what you love?[^1]

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.
